Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Somalia predominantly use paper-based records such as occurrence books (OB)/station diaries, crime registers, lost property registers, lock-up registers, and prisoners property registers, as per Somali Police Basic Recruit Curriculum from UNSOM, which trains on 'police books and forms' without mentioning digital tools. Official Somali Police site notes UNODC-supported digital crime statistics system populated with 'reported data' from police across Somalia (including rural posts), implying aggregation from paper at higher levels rather than direct digital entry at stations. Recent IECMS (Oct 2025) launch replaces historical paper-based processes but targets CID, prosecutors, courts, prisons—not routine station case files; rural rollout unlikely given fragmented infrastructure and calls for centralized systems. Prisons still paper-based per reports; similar for rural police. No rural-specific digital pilots found; score 1 as broad evidence points to paper at facility level.

revision_notes: Confirmed score 1. Verified cited sources: police.gov.so page and the UNSOM Basic Recruit Curriculum both support paper-based station-level record-keeping, with national crime statistics aggregated from reported (paper) data. Fresh search found Somalia's Justice Sector Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS), launched in Mogadishu on 9 October 2025, but this explicitly covers the Criminal Investigation Department, Prosecutor's Office, courts and prisons, not routine rural police-station record capture. A Puntland regional CID information-system upgrade (EUCAP Somalia support) likewise targets CID data flows to headquarters rather than station-level paper registers. No evidence was found of digital data capture at the point of service in rural police stations. Score confirmed at 1.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Somalia continue to rely on paper-based record-keeping, including occurrence books, station diaries, crime registers, lost-property registers and prisoners' property registers, in line with the training given in the Somali Police Force's Basic Recruit Curriculum, which covers 'police books and forms' with no reference to digital tools. The Somali Police Force publishes national crime statistics compiled from data reported by police stations across the country, indicating aggregation from paper records rather than direct digital entry at station level. Somalia's new Justice Sector Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS), launched in Mogadishu in October 2025 with US government and IDLO support, digitises case files for the Criminal Investigation Department, Prosecutor's Office, courts and prisons, but does not extend to routine record-keeping in rural police stations. IT upgrades in regional Criminal Investigation Department offices, such as those supported by EUCAP Somalia in Puntland, likewise focus on CID data flows rather than station-level paper registers. Data capture at the point of service in rural police stations therefore remains entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Somalia predominantly use paper-based recording for administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. According to the 2018 World Bank EMIS report, data collection relies on enumerators visiting ~1,300 schools (75% coverage, including rural) with printed 13-page census questionnaires filled out on paper; schools provide info verbally or on paper, with no federal digital tools at point-of-service. Forms are aggregated manually at regional/state levels before central digital entry into PINEAPPLES software. State variations exist (e.g., some Galmudug rural head teachers upload online), but federal/national picture shows paper default. The MoECHE 2020 Yearbook claims head teachers enter data via online EMIS, but lacks methodological details distinguishing rural paper vs digital and aligns with prior paper-upward model; remote rural data hard to verify due to access/security. Digital pilots like UNICEF/World Vision Digital Attendance App (DAA) limited to 3 schools in Puntland (urban Garowe?), needing $100k to scale; not representative of rural majority. Barriers: insecurity limiting rural access, low incentives for non-state schools (majority), poor infrastructure/power/mobile data in rural/nomadic areas, staff shortages, no universal devices/training. National ambition for decentralized EMIS (ESSP 2018-20, recent policy) contrasts with rural reality of annual paper censuses and sporadic records; no evidence majority rural schools routinely use digital at point-of-service (score 1). World Bank EMIS Report; MoECHE 2020 Yearbook; DAA Pilot

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) reassessed. Verified sources: the World Bank EMIS status report (based on c.2018 data) and the Ministry of Education's Annual Statistics Yearbook confirm paper-based annual census collection with manual aggregation upward, particularly from rural areas. A fresh search found a Global Partnership for Education blog (February 2024) describing a CARE International Somalia programme in which headteachers such as 'Abdi', at a GPE-ESPIG-supported school, now enter student and teacher data directly into the online EMIS themselves rather than filing paper records, corroborating the original comment's note that 'some Galmudug rural head teachers upload online' alongside the UNICEF/World Vision Digital Attendance App pilot in Puntland. A 2023 GPE sector review still finds EMIS 'limited in geographic/subsector coverage', so paper remains the majority practice, but the evidence of multiple, if scattered, instances of direct digital data entry at rural facility level is inconsistent with 'Entirely paper' and better matches 'Mostly paper - some digital'. Revised to 2.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Somalia predominantly rely on paper-based record-keeping for enrolment, attendance and administrative data, with annual school census data collected on paper questionnaires by enumerators and aggregated upward before entry into the national Education Management Information System (EMIS). A Global Partnership for Education-funded programme implemented by CARE International Somalia has, however, trained headteachers in GPE-supported schools, including in rural areas, to enter student and teacher data directly into the online EMIS themselves, replacing manual paper filing at school level. Similar isolated digital pilots include head teachers uploading data online in Galmudug and a Digital Attendance App piloted in a small number of Puntland schools. These pockets of direct digital data capture remain a minority nationally: the Ministry of Education's Annual Statistics Yearbook and a 2023 sector review both note that EMIS coverage and capacity remain geographically limited, with rural schools continuing to face significant reporting gaps. Data capture in rural primary schools is therefore best characterised as mostly paper-based with pockets of direct digital entry.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Somalia predominantly record patient data using standardized paper registers (12 types covering OPD, IPD, immunization, MCH, etc.), with monthly aggregated summary forms sent to district HMIS officers for entry into the national DHIS2 system.WHO HIS Assessment Although DHIS2 enables direct entry via computer/tablet, in practice most facilities—including rural primary health units and health centres—use paper at point-of-service, as confirmed by 2022 field visits to rural sites like Dayah HC (Galmudug).WHO HIS Assessment No nationwide EMR exists; WHO eHealth profile indicates N/A EHR adoption at primary facilities.WHO eHealth Profile Digital pilots include OGOW app (Puntland vaccinations via tablets), IDSR tracker (2023), electronic immunization registry, and donor projects like CaafimaadPlus C+ DDS (Ogow Health, live in 43 south-central facilities incl. rural since 2024 for patient records/dashboard), RAAD EMR (scaling to 40 clinics).ReliefWeb CaafimaadPlus These are isolated, partner-funded, not scaled as standard across most rural clinics. Barriers: Limited rural electricity/internet/devices, HMIS officer shortages (58-70% districts lack), staff multi-tasking (95%), conflict/displacement, donor fragmentation.WHO HIS Assessment National policy (HIS strategy, EPHS) aims for EMR/digital HIS (2023-26), but rural PoS remains paper-dominant with digital limited to aggregation/pilots—clear gap between ambition and reality.

revision_notes: Confirmed score 2. The WHO HIS assessment cited in the original comments, describing paper registers with monthly aggregation into DHIS2 at district level, is consistent with 'mostly paper - some digital'. Fresh search confirms continued scaling of point-of-service digital pilots: the CaafimaadPlus Digitalised Data System (C+ DDS), which began in mid-2024 in five facilities, had by April 2026 expanded to more than 40 facilities across nine regions and over 25 districts, feeding directly into the government's DHIS2 platform in real time; UNICEF and the University of Oslo's HISP Centre signed a new three-year DHIS2 support agreement in August 2025. A facility-based study (October-December 2024, 36 public facilities in Banadir) found overall routine health information data quality of only 65.3%, consistent with continued heavy reliance on paper registers and manual processes at facility level nationally. These pilots remain a minority of Somalia's rural primary healthcare facilities, so the national picture remains predominantly paper with a growing but still partial digital footprint. Score confirmed at 2.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Somalia predominantly record patient data on standardised paper registers covering outpatient care, in-patient care, immunisation and maternal and child health, with monthly summary forms aggregated by district health information officers into the national DHIS2 system rather than being entered digitally at the point of service. A facility-based study of 36 public health facilities in Banadir (October-December 2024) found overall routine health information data quality of 65.3%, consistent with continued reliance on manual, paper-based processes at facility level. Donor-funded digital pilots are expanding, however: the CaafimaadPlus Digitalised Data System (C+ DDS), which began in mid-2024 in five facilities, had grown by 2026 to more than 40 facilities across nine regions and over 25 districts, capturing patient records directly on handheld devices and feeding data in real time into the government's DHIS2 platform. UNICEF and the University of Oslo's HISP Centre signed a new three-year agreement in August 2025 to further strengthen DHIS2 and build local capacity. These initiatives remain concentrated in a minority of Somalia's rural clinics, so the overall national picture is one of paper-based data capture with a growing but still partial digital presence.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (Degmada/local municipalities) rely on paper forms for births; extremely low completeness (3.5% children <5 registered, 0.3% certificates; 2020 SHDS, no rural-urban gap Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada). Home/nomadic births undocumented. UNFPA 2021: No national CRVS office, decentralized, policy for digital repository but unimplemented; fragility/infrastructure gaps block rollout UNFPA CRVS Profile. Digital pilots: OpenCRVS in 30 districts (many rural), 160 hospitals linked; 28k+ births registered digitally at point-of-service to central DB (2026) OpenCRVS. Launched 19 districts incl. rural (e.g., Abudwaq, Hudur, Kismayo) Aug 2025 SONNA. Barriers: Insecurity, nomadic lifestyle, poor connectivity, low awareness. Gap: CRVS policy/law (2021+), 2024-29 plan ambitious but pilots cover minority facilities; majority rural remains paper-based.

revision_notes: Confirmed score 2. Original sources (UNFPA CRVS profile, ecoi.net/IRB report, OpenCRVS country story) confirm extremely low birth registration completeness (3.5% of under-5s, 2020 SHDS) and continued reliance on paper-based local registration outside a limited digital footprint. Fresh search confirms the Ministry of Interior, Federal Affairs and Reconciliation publicly launched a 'Unified Digital Civil Registration Service' in 19 districts across Jubbaland, South West, Hirshabelle, Galmudug and Northeastern State on Africa CRVS Day, 10 August 2025, enabling local registration offices to capture births, deaths, marriages and divorces digitally with real-time transmission to a central database (Biometric Update and Ecofin Agency, 10-12 August 2025). The OpenCRVS country page reports this has since grown to around 30 districts and 160 linked hospitals, with over 28,000 births registered digitally at the point of occurrence. As Somalia has roughly 90 districts nationally, this represents genuine but still partial point-of-service digitisation, covering perhaps a third of districts, with the majority of rural registry offices still paper-based. revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Somalia have historically relied on paper-based birth, death and marriage registration, with completeness extremely low (around 3.5% of children under five registered and 0.3% holding a birth certificate, per the 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey) and no rural-urban gap in completeness. On Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Day, 10 August 2025, Somalia's Ministry of Interior, Federal Affairs and Reconciliation launched a Unified Digital Civil Registration Service, initially operational in 19 districts across the Jubbaland, South West, Hirshabelle, Galmudug and Northeastern State federal member states, enabling local offices to register births, deaths, marriages and divorces digitally with data transmitted in real time to a central database; some health facilities without computers were equipped with tablets for this purpose. Built on the OpenCRVS platform with UNICEF and German government support, the system has since expanded to around 30 districts and 160 linked hospitals, with more than 28,000 births registered digitally at the point of occurrence. As Somalia has roughly 90 districts nationally, this represents genuine but still partial coverage, with the majority of rural civil registry offices continuing to depend on paper-based registration.
